extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP litigators, in‑house counsel and patent owners considering or litigating before the Unified Patent Court (UPC)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and legal standards for bringing, defending, and managing patent infringement and revocation proceedings before the Unified Patent Court (UPC), including jurisdiction, timing, claim construction, remedies, enforcement, costs and invalidity risks. Focused on strategic decision-making for Unitary and European (bundle) patents in the UPC system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction for infringement actions (forum shopping under Art.33 UPCA)
rubrics_metrics.description: When bringing an infringement action, the claimant may bring the action before the Local Division hosted by the Contracting Member State where the infringement occurred (Art.33(1)(a) UPCA) or where the defendant (or one of multiple defendants) has its residence (Art.33(1)(b) UPCA), creating a system of 'parallel competence' and enabling forum shopping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish jurisdiction based on place of infringement, it is sufficient to provide a plausible allegation that an infringement occurred in that Contracting Member State (not a conclusive argument at the filing stage). Parallel competence between Local Divisions paves the way for forum shopping; consider Local Division caseloads, panel composition, and procedural culture when choosing venue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi‑defendant jurisdiction and 'anchor defendant' concept (Art.33(1)(b) UPCA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Art.33(1)(b) UPCA, it is possible to bring an infringement action before the same Local Division against multiple defendants, provided the defendants have a commercial relationship and the action relates to the same alleged infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The requirements under Art.33(1)(b) are less strict than Brussels I bis Art.8(1); the domicile of an 'anchor defendant' can provide the option to sue the entire group before that Local Division. Use commercial-relationship facts to establish connection; consider current case law of Local Divisions on the scope of this ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Court structure and competence: Local/Regional vs Central Division
rubrics_metrics.description: Local and Regional Divisions of the Court of First Instance are competent for infringement, while the Central Division is competent for revocation (central revocation actions). Panels may sit in multinational composition per Art.8 UPCA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local Divisions handle infringement and may also hear counterclaims for revocation or refer them to the Central Division; when strategizing, consider whether to keep issues localized or refer to central revocation (which has erga omnes effect). Panel composition (national vs multinational balance) can affect predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: UPC territorial scope ('UPC Land') and Member States coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC Land covers the UPC Member States (18 countries as of Sept 1, 2024 / March 2026 reporting), allowing injunctions based on Unitary Patents or validated European (bundle) patents for those Member States; the UPC can revoke European patents for the whole UPC Land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing relief and risks, consider which countries are in UPC Land (affects territorial reach of injunctions and revocation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unitary Patent: request timing and renewal fee model (True Top 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: After grant of a European patent, the patentee can request unitary effect (Unitary Patent) within one month after publication of the mention of grant (practical variations exist among Local Divisions); renewal fees use the 'True Top 4' model (correspond to sum of renewal fees of four most frequently validated countries).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unitary Patent simplifies validation and annuities but may be costlier (True Top 4 includes UK in calculation, raising renewal fees). Weigh countries where protection is needed, cost, and litigation risk before opting for unitary effect; timing for requesting unitary effect may vary in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive UPC competence for Unitary Patent and concurrent jurisdiction for bundle patents during transitional period
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC has exclusive competence for infringement and revocation actions concerning the Unitary Patent. For European bundle patents there is concurrent jurisdiction with national courts during a transitional period of seven years (extendable by seven years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent proprietors may 'opt‑out' bundle patents from UPC jurisdiction up to one month before the end of the transitional period (opt-out inadmissible if action already brought before the UPC). Withdrawal of opt-out is possible unless a national action was already brought during the transitional regime. Consider opt-out to avoid 'central' revocation risk, but be mindful that opt‑out can allow national nullity actions that preclude later UPC central actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of national utility models (e.g., German) alongside Unitary Patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Patentees choosing Unitary Patent (which gives UPC exclusive jurisdiction) who do not want to lose access to national courts may consider filing additional national patents or utility models (e.g., German utility models provide quick, cost‑efficient protection for products and uses but not for process claims and have a 10‑year term).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility models can supplement unitary protection where national remedies are desired; assess technical field, allowed claim types, and product life cycle before pursuing utility models.

rubrics_metrics.name: UPC long‑arm jurisdiction for up to 39 EPC countries if defendant domiciled in UPC Land
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC may hear infringement actions with respect to EPC countries where the European patent is in force (including some non‑UPC states) if the defendant or an 'anchor defendant' is domiciled in UPC Land (Art.4(1), Art.8(1), Art.71b Brussels I bis Regulation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows centralized injunctive relief for many EPC states in one UPC action when jurisdictional conditions are met; evaluate where defendants are domiciled and whether an anchor defendant exists to maximize territorial reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity competence where alleged infringement concerns EU non‑UPC Member States (Art.24 no.4 Brussels I bis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the UPC is competent for infringement concerning acts in EU Member States that are non‑UPC, the national courts of those non‑UPC Member States have exclusive competence for the question of validity of those parts of the European patent (Art.24 no.4 Brussels I bis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The UPC may stay infringement proceedings in light of an invalidity defense to allow decisions by national courts of non‑UPC Member States. Strategically, defendants may file national nullity actions to challenge validity for those territories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity and infringement for EPC non‑EU states (different treatment)
rubrics_metrics.description: For EPC countries that are non‑EU Member States, a court of the EU Member State where the defendant is domiciled may be competent for infringement concerning acts in those non‑EU EPC countries and may have competence to decide on invalidity with inter partes effect; the treatment differs because Art.24 no.4 Brussels I bis does not apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local Divisions have considered UPC validity of non‑EU parts in practice, but defendants should present differences between national law of the non‑EU state and the law applied by the UPC when arguing non‑UPC validity distinctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant must file counterclaim for revocation to have UPC address invalidity (Art.65(1) UPCA)
rubrics_metrics.description: To argue that the patent‑in‑suit is invalid before the UPC, the defendant must file a counterclaim for revocation; without a counterclaim, the invalidity defense does not need to be addressed by the UPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a counterclaim converts the validity question into a revocation action with potentially erga omnes effect; failure to counterclaim risks the UPC proceeding without addressing invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement of cross‑border injunctions may require recognition in third states
rubrics_metrics.description: Enforcement of cross‑border injunctions within UPC Land (e.g., penalty payments) may be subject to additional requirements such as recognition of the underlying decision in the respective third state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if the UPC issues broad cross‑border relief, practical enforcement outside UPC Land or in third states may be constrained; plan enforcement strategy accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Further long‑arm grounds and anchor‑intermediary debate (Brussels I bis Art.8(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: Long‑arm jurisdiction may be given for defendants domiciled outside UPC Land if the defendant acts together with an 'anchor defendant' domiciled in UPC Land, but details (e.g., whether an intermediary can serve as anchor) are subject to ongoing debate and CJEU referral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor pending CJEU referrals and Local Division case law when relying on intermediary/anchor theories to establish jurisdiction for non‑UPC domiciled defendants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Long‑arm jurisdiction for damages outside the EU (non‑EU defendant and Lugano Convention implications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Against a defendant neither domiciled in an EU Member State nor in a Lugano Convention Member, the UPC can have international jurisdiction for damages arising outside the EU (e.g., UK) where property of the defendant is located in a UPC Member State and the dispute has sufficient connection to that Member State (Art.71b No.2, No.3 Brussels I bis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UPC competence for injunctive relief in such cases may be limited to UPC Land; consider Lugano/Art.73 interplay and whether national courts or recognition requirements affect remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: UPC speed and 'Rocket Docket' timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rules of Procedure emphasize that the final oral hearing on infringement and validity at first instance shall typically take place within one year; empirical averages reported are ~406 days for main infringement decisions and ~96 days for preliminary injunctions after year one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect condensed timetables; structure evidence and witness preparation accordingly. Average timelines are illustrative; actual times depend on case complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time extensions and strict adherence to RoP deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Time extensions for RoP deadlines are theoretically possible but the UPC is rather reluctant to grant them; extensions are typically only for exceptional circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan to meet deadlines; be cautious relying on extensions. Confidentiality submissions and negotiations over 'confidentiality clubs' can be used to create delay but will require justification and may or may not succeed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on additional submissions and procedural control (R.9, R.332 RoP)
rubrics_metrics.description: The written procedure is limited to submissions expressly mentioned in the RoP. Before conclusion of the written procedure the judge‑rapporteur may allow a further exchange upon a reasoned request; after conclusion no further written submissions are provided, but the court may issue procedural orders under R.9 or R.332 at any stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use early-stage submissions strategically and seek judge‑rapporteur permission where needed. Procedural orders can direct parties to provide clarification or evidence, so anticipate judicially requested supplementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction (PI) requirements and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: In PI proceedings the applicant must prove: entitlement to initiate proceedings, that the patent is valid, that the patent is infringed, that the requirement of urgency is fulfilled, and that the balance of interests favors the applicant. For entitlement, validity and infringement a prima facie analysis suffices ('at least more likely than not' >50%). The defendant bears the burden to prove invalidity in inter partes PI proceedings. Urgency and balance of interests require a higher burden than prima facie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate 'sufficient degree of certainty' for the first three elements; show timely action to satisfy urgency (courts examine delay and negligence). A PI may be necessary to maintain the status quo and will be denied if it would disturb long‑established market status. If PI granted, main action must be filed within 31 calendar days or 20 working days (longer applies) or PI will be revoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction / UPC infringement test ('broadest meaningful interpretation')
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC applies a broad German‑style claim construction: claim features receive their 'broadest meaningful interpretation' focusing on technical function in the context of the technical problem. Claims are interpreted using the description and drawings as aids, not limited to preferred embodiments, and from the viewpoint of the person skilled in the art. The same test applies to Unitary and European bundle patents; a uniform standard for doctrine of equivalents remains to be established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drafting/arguing, rely on description/drawings to support broad interpretation or to limit scope; do not assume literal wording alone controls. Expect UPC to consider patentee's own lexicon if specification defines terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies available and injunction tendencies (Art.63 UPCA)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the UPC finds validity and infringement, it may grant permanent injunctive relief (Art.63), corrective measures like recall/destruction (Art.64), rendering of information (Art.67) and damages (Art.68). Current case law interprets Art.63 narrowly, but injunctive relief tends to follow regularly; the court has discretion and may deny injunctions on disproportionality grounds (Art.42 UPCA), but defendants face a high hurdle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendants wanting to avoid injunctions should prepare strong disproportionality arguments and evidentiary proof; burden of demonstration lies with infringer. Plaintiffs should routinely request injunctions where infringement/validity established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages under Art.68 UPCA and procedural timings for claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Art.68 provides two options for damages: (a) consider all appropriate aspects including negative economic consequences (lost profits), unfair profits, and, where appropriate, non‑economic elements; or (b) set a lump sum on the basis of elements such as royalties. A damage claim may not be brought more than five years after awareness of last fact justifying the action (Art.72 UPCA). To pursue damages after a merits decision, the party must lodge the application no later than one year from service of the final decision (R.126 RoP).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is limited UPC precedent on damage calculation; expect fact‑intensive assessments and possible separate proceedings to determine amount. Consider intervening EPO/national proceedings that might affect entitlement and quantum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security for enforcement and its frequency/criteria (R.352, R.118.8, R.211.5 RoP)
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC may require security for enforcement (deposit, bank guarantee, etc.) to compensate the losing party if a decision is enforced and later revoked. Security has been ordered infrequently (6% of main infringement actions, 36% of PI proceedings as of March 31, 2025). The request for enforcement security must be substantiated by the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts look at claimant's financial position and enforcement law of claimant's domicile. Amounts typically cover proceedings costs, enforcement costs and likely harm; valuation is difficult so courts base security on value in dispute unless defendant provides detailed harm estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost rules: 'loser pays', ceilings, and cost security (R.152, R.158, R.370.6 RoP)
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC applies a 'loser pays' approach but the loser reimburses only 'reasonable fees up to a certain ceiling' (R.152.1-.2 RoP), with ceilings determined by the value of the proceedings (court sets value, reflecting plaintiff's objective interest; cf. R.370.6 RoP). Ceilings apply to representation costs; other expenses (prior art research, translations, experts) are additional. The court may order cost security under R.158 if a party's financial position raises legitimate concern about recoverability/enforceability of costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When calculating cost risk, account for potential six‑ or seven‑digit reimbursement claims under 'loser pays' and prepare to seek or oppose cost security early. Under R.158 the court examines facts and arguments; relative financial position alone is not dispositive, e.g., limited funding of enforcement vehicles is not per se a reason to order security.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity risks: central revocation, counterclaims and parallel proceedings (EPO, national)
rubrics_metrics.description: The UPC enables 'central' attacks that can revoke patents erga omnes. Central revocation actions and counterclaims for revocation can run in parallel. Parallel EPO opposition proceedings do not block revocation actions at the UPC; an EPO decision may overrule a UPC decision and vice versa. If UPC and EPO outcomes differ, limitations from both may need to be considered. Parallel national nullity proceedings are possible during the transitional period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees should be wary of 'all eggs in one basket' risk with central revocation; defendants should consider parallel strategies (UPC counterclaim, EPO opposition, national nullity) to maximize invalidity chances and legal certainty. Monitor timing and strategic interactions between forums; UPC may stay proceedings if rapid EPO decision is likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stay rules and interplay with national courts during transitional period (Brussels I bis, RoP)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the transitional period the UPC and national courts have concurrent jurisdiction for bundle patents; where proceedings involve the same cause of action and same parties the UPC shall stay (Brussels I bis Art.29–32, R.295 RoP). In related cases the UPC may stay at its discretion; factors include degree of identity of cause of action, closely related parties, and more advanced stage of national proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When planning strategy, assess whether parallel national proceedings exist or are likely and whether they will trigger a UPC stay. Use timing to your advantage: the party that files first in the appropriate forum can influence whether UPC jurisdiction becomes available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cost comparisons and practical cost drivers
rubrics_metrics.description: UPC infringement actions can offer very good value when compared to multiple national EU actions, UK national litigation and US litigation. Key cost advantages include limited discovery, condensed trial format (one‑day style), limited expert role, and only UPC representatives required (no separate trial counsel like UK barristers). Main costs remain attorney fees; court fees are generally moderate (< EUR 50,000 in a standard matter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use UPC to centralize relief when territorial reach and cost tradeoffs favor a single action. However, consider potential 'loser pays' reimbursement risk and prepare budget for representation fees and additional expenses (prior‑art searches, translations, experts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical success rates and caveats
rubrics_metrics.description: As of March 2026, 45% of main infringement actions decided by Court of First Instance ended in favor of the plaintiff; 37% of defendant successes were based on complete revocation; preliminary injunction success rate ~60%. Enforcement security ordered in 6% of successful main actions and 36% of successful PI proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat statistics cautiously: data set is limited, many appeals pending, and parallel EPO oppositions may change outcomes. Use success‑rate data for high‑level strategy but not as deterministic predictors.
